intro: The pilgrims’ hymn walks slowly into the music of Venus’s mountain, then returns with the quick notes still circling it. In Sousa’s arrangement, played by the United States Marine Band, clarinets inherit the strings’ racing lines.

sections.label: A · The pilgrims’ hymn
sections.mNote: Clarinet, bassoon and horns begin a quiet B♭-major hymn

sections.label: A′ · Brass take the hymn
sections.mNote: Broad brass phrases stand above running first clarinets

sections.label: B · Inside Venus’s mountain
sections.mNote: Quick clarinet figures pass to the upper woodwind

sections.label: C · A clarinet in the hush
sections.mNote: A solo clarinet sings among delicate upper-wind figures

sections.label: B′ · The song to Venus returns
sections.mNote: The broad song returns in B♭ above flowing lower parts

sections.label: A′ · Pilgrims beneath the quick notes
sections.mNote: The hymn returns while the first clarinets keep running

sections.label: A″ · The hymn fills the band
sections.mNote: Full brass and upper winds carry the closing B♭-major hymn

relations.label: The Venus song returns higher
relations.basis: The broad song in the fast Venusberg section is restated in the renewed fast span. The five-semitone upward pitch-class shift is consistent with its move to another tonal level; the listening notes distinguish this song from the pilgrims’ hymn. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 34.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift +5 semitones and time offset 174 s (cache/form/wagner-tannhauser-overture.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The pilgrims’ hymn returns
relations.basis: The overture’s closing frame restores the pilgrims’ hymn after the Venusberg music. The earlier excerpt comes from the hymn’s first broad statement, while the later one follows the return marked near 665 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.934, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 527 s (cache/form/wagner-tannhauser-overture.txt, candidate 5; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Pilgrims on the road
cues.text: The hymn begins quietly in clarinet, bassoon and horns. Its long B♭-major phrases belong to the pilgrims travelling to Rome in the opera. Sousa keeps the scoring spare: the band’s brightest instruments wait while the procession comes into view.
cues.evidence: John Philip Sousa’s band transcription, printed p. 1, Andante maestoso: solo B♭ clarinet, bassoons, horns, lower clarinets and bass. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240. Dramatic identification: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinets around the brass
cues.text: The brass give the hymn a broad, firm tread. Above it, the first clarinets run through continuous semiquavers, taking the part Wagner gives to the orchestral strings. The hymn holds its long notes while the surrounding music hurries on.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, opening full hymn, including printed pp. 10–12: brass melody and first-clarinet semiquavers in 3/4.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A disastrous song contest
cues.text: Tannhäuser leaves Venus’s realm, then sings her praises at the Wartburg song contest. The other singers turn on him. Elisabeth protects him, and he joins the pilgrims bound for Rome.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note, plot synopsis and account of the overture: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user.

cues.title: The mountain stirs quietly
cues.text: Venus’s music begins in little running clarinet figures, answered by the upper woodwind. The bass and heavy brass fall away. Wagner changes the hymn’s three-beat metre to common time and marks Allegro, but the new world slips in softly.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 19–20, bar 82 onwards: Allegro, change from 3/4 to common time, lower-clarinet figures and pp upper-wind answers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clarinet among flickering notes
cues.text: The solo clarinet has a long, supple melody while flute, piccolo and E♭ clarinet keep little figures moving around it. The bass is largely silent. Even in this hush, Venus’s music never becomes as still as the pilgrims’ hymn.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 39–42, quieter episode at rehearsal D: solo clarinet and upper-wind figures, with extended rests in bass and brass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Venus receives another song
cues.text: The broad song in praise of Venus returns in B♭ major. Flowing lines in the lower clarinets, saxophones and euphonium keep moving beneath it. This is Tannhäuser the singer again, finding a generous tune for the world he struggles to leave.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 49–50, rehearsal E, Tempo I and B♭-major restatement. Mandel identifies the central broad melody as Tannhäuser’s hymn to Venus.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Whistles at the Paris Opéra
cues.text: For Paris in 1861, Wagner puts the ballet in Act I. Members of the Jockey Club want their dancing later in the evening. Whistles and catcalls wreck the performances; after three nights, Wagner withdraws the opera.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note, account of the Paris production, first-act ballet, Jockey Club disruption and withdrawal after three performances.

cues.title: The pilgrims keep walking
cues.text: The hymn returns in the middle and lower wind parts. The first clarinets still run above it. Wagner brings back the procession without clearing away the mountain’s restless movement; the two kinds of music now occupy the same road.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 62–66, returning hymn and continuing first-clarinet semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wagner still owes the world
cues.text: On 23 January 1883, Cosima writes in her diary: “He says he still owes the world Tannhäuser.” Wagner has spent nearly forty years returning to the opera. Even now, it refuses to leave him alone.
cues.evidence: Cosima Wagner’s diary, 23 January 1883, quoted in Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony programme note: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user.

cues.title: The hymn takes the sky
cues.text: The upper winds and full brass carry the hymn in B♭ major. The clarinets continue their quick figures almost as if they have been absorbed into the procession. Sousa gives the long melody the whole breadth of the band.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 76–79, rehearsal H, Assai stretto: expanded wind and brass doublings over continuous first clarinets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The brass broaden the hymn
transitions.how: The hymn stays in B♭ major and keeps its three-beat tread. Brass instruments take its long notes while the first clarinets acquire a continuous running part. Low instruments mark out the bass beneath the two speeds: the procession has gained both weight and a restless halo.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, opening build and full hymn, including printed pp. 10–12: B♭ major, 3/4, brass melody, first-clarinet semiquavers.

transitions.title: Quick notes emerge from the hush
transitions.how: The B♭-major hymn dwindles into sustained wind notes. At Allegro, 3/4 gives way to common time and the lower clarinets begin a soft rising figure. Flute, oboe and upper clarinets answer with chromatic turns. The bass rests: the new music arrives without a heavy first step.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 19–20, bar 82 and following: Allegro, common time, clarinet figures, upper-wind pp entries, bass rests.

transitions.title: The clarinet sings through the hush
transitions.to: C · A clarinet in the hush
transitions.how: The forceful chords give way to quiet falling and rising wind figures. The low bass drops out, and the solo clarinet finds a sustained line among the flute, piccolo and E♭ clarinet’s smaller notes. At Un poco ritenuto the phrase briefly holds back, leaving the melody suspended above its accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 39–42, approach to rehearsal D and the clarinet episode.

transitions.title: F releases the song into B♭
transitions.from: C · A clarinet in the hush
transitions.to: B′ · The song to Venus returns
transitions.how: The band holds F-major harmony, then repeats it in short, accented chords. F prepares B♭ as its dominant. At Tempo I the Venus song returns in B♭ major, with flowing quavers in the lower clarinets, saxophones and euphonium beneath the broader upper melody.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 49–50, sustained dominant preparation and rehearsal E, Tempo I.

transitions.title: The hymn returns under running clarinets
transitions.from: B′ · The song to Venus returns
transitions.to: A′ · Pilgrims beneath the quick notes
transitions.how: The fast music thins out towards B♭ major. The hymn returns in the lower clarinets, horns and saxophones, with long supporting bass notes. Above it, the first clarinets keep their semiquavers. The pilgrims walk through the movement left behind by Venus’s music.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 62–66: returning hymn in the middle and low winds, running first clarinets and sustained bass support.

transitions.title: The whole band carries the hymn
transitions.from: A′ · Pilgrims beneath the quick notes
transitions.to: A″ · The hymn fills the band
transitions.how: At rehearsal H, marked Assai stretto, the upper winds and full brass join the B♭-major hymn. The bass reinforces its steps while the first clarinets keep running. Long notes spread from the low brass to the top of the wind section, with the restless accompaniment still inside them.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 76–79: rehearsal H, Assai stretto, enlarged wind and brass doublings and continuing first-clarinet figures.

source.title: Wagner, Tannhäuser Overture, concert-band full score, arranged by John Philip Sousa
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–91; opening, A, Allegro, D, E, returning chorale and H. Alto clarinet is grouped with clarinets, and flugelhorns with cornets. Passage timings are approximate.

timeline.note: Bassoons, solo clarinet and horns share the hymn above alto clarinet, bass clarinet and tuba.
Oboe and euphonium broaden the melodic line; saxophones and low reeds thicken its support.
Brass proclaim the hymn while first clarinets supply the rapid upper figures.
Quiet clarinet runs initiate the fast music; upper woodwinds answer above lighter lower-wind support.
The Venus song expands through the band above running reed figures and stronger brass support.
Solo clarinet sustains the line against flute, piccolo and E♭ clarinet figures; heavy brass withdraw.
The Venus song returns with full-band doublings above moving saxophones, low clarinets and euphoniums.
Lower winds and horns restore the hymn beneath the first clarinets’ continuing rapid line.
The full brass hymn gains upper-wind doublings while clarinet figuration continues around its long notes.
Running figures settle into the band’s sustained final chords and timpani-supported close.

composer.epithet: He hid the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth and taught it to remember everything his characters wanted to forget.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no success worth mentioning. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons calling across the strings’ storm. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to persuade somebody to stage his music.

He had grown up inside the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies supplied the sounds; Theodor Weinlig supplied counterpoint lessons in 1831. Jobs followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen remained unperformed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, collapsed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
